episodes.label: evidence-sft-r2-paired-r1-vs-r2-baseline-city-shade
episodes.notes:
[chapter-p001] Twelve streets in Bellwick had mature trees; twelve nearby streets did not. Sensors measured air temperature at pedestrian height between noon and 6 p.m. on ten dry days. Shaded streets were cooler on average, but the difference was largest late in the afternoon. These measurements describe the sampled streets and weather; they do not establish how much planting a new tree would immediately cool another neighborhood.

[chapter-p002] Shade reduces sunlight absorbed by pavement and by people standing beneath the canopy. Trees release water vapor through their leaves, which can cool the surrounding air. An awning provides shade without releasing water, while a tree with sparse foliage may release water without providing much shelter from direct sun. The study did not separately measure the contribution of either mechanism.

[chapter-p003] Tree cover was unevenly distributed. Older residential streets had wider planting strips and more mature canopies; several shopping streets had narrow sidewalks and dense underground utilities. Some of the hottest blocks contained the busiest bus stops. Counting trees across an entire district concealed differences in where people actually waited or walked. The authors suggested measuring shade along common routes, not merely reporting a district-wide tree total.

[chapter-p004] Planting was only the start of the proposed response. Young trees needed watering and maintenance before providing substantial shade; some sites could not accommodate their roots. Temporary shade structures were proposed while planners investigated longer-term options. This was not a recommendation to replace existing mature trees with structures. The report warned that choosing one fast-growing species everywhere could leave the whole planting program vulnerable to the same pest.

[chapter-p005] The authors described the findings as an initial local comparison, not a forecast. They had not measured winter conditions, unusually humid days, indoor temperatures, or health outcomes. They proposed repeating the measurements in another summer and including observations of how people used the shaded routes. Whether a particular intervention improved residents' daily experience would still depend on access, maintenance, and where the shade fell.
episodes.summary: In Bellwick, mature tree streets were cooler than treeless ones, but planting did not immediately cool neighborhoods. Shade reduced pavement and pedestrian heat absorption, yet an awning provides shade without releasing water. Tree cover was unevenly distributed, so counting trees concealed differences in where people waited. Planting required watering and maintenance before providing substantial shade.

episodes.label: evidence-sft-r2-paired-r1-vs-r2-baseline-exceptions
episodes.notes:
[exceptions-p01] Ticket-system outage: agents keep offline log with ticket identifiers and timestamps; after recovery, import log without overwriting newer activity.
[exceptions-p02] Suspected duplicates: mark as related, retain both records until reviewer decides whether merge is safe.
[exceptions-p03] Weekly review: compare ticket-system counts with offline-log counts; any difference remains unresolved until cause documented.
[exceptions-p04] Support lead approves routine corrections; deleting a record or changing a customer-visible deadline requires approval from operations manager.
episodes.summary:
- Ticket-system outage: import offline log without overwriting.
- Suspected duplicates: mark related, retain both until reviewer decides.
- Weekly review: compare counts, resolve differences only after cause documented.
- Support lead approves corrections; deleting records or changing deadlines requires operations manager approval.
